newsitem.title: USA: Copper prices climb to six month high.
newsitem.headline: Copper prices climb to six month high.

text.p: Copper prices rose to their highest level in six months Wednesday, aided partly by the improving economic outlook in Europe and Japan.

"The price action has been impressive and combined with gains in other base metals prices recently suggests that economic growth in Europe and Japan may be reviving faster than expected," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
Traders said there was concern that nearby supplies were tight while some suggested China might buy copper soon to replenish strategic stocks.
"It is very tight moving into the peak demand period of March-June," said analyst Robin Bahr of London Metal Exchange brokers Brandeis.

The copper market has been recovering steadily during the last four months after a price collapse in the first half of 1996 linked to Sumitomo Corp.'s dismissal of trader Yasuo Hamanaka. A hoard of stocks he controlled had kept prices high and his exit triggered a rapid decline in prices.
March copper on New York's Commodity Exchange (COMEX) closed 2.40 cents higher at 112.00 cents a pound after setting a new six-month peak of 112.80 cents earlier in the day.

Coffee prices on New York's Coffee, Sugar, Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) also rose sharply, resuming a strong upward trend after a short-lived setback Tuesday. Heavy buying by commodity funds helped spark the strong advance amid continued concern about tight stocks.

Analysts noted news that Brazil's exporter group Abecafe had pegged the coming 1997-98 harvest at 23.2 million 60-kilogram (132-pound) bags, slightly below the government's 1996-97 estimate of 25 million.
"The Brazil estimate is still lower than last year's and it points to a deficit situation," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt.
Abecafe's secretary-general said Wednesday that Brazil is likely to see a production deficit of at least 4 million bags in 1997-98.

"(Total) demand for Brazilian coffee is of the order of 28 million bags, and this is a conservative estimate," Jose Sette told a news conference in Sao Paolo, Brazil. "We will have a deficit of more than 4 million bags, nearly 5 million."

Additionally, Platt said monthly inventory data showing a modest increase in U.S. consumer coffee stocks was also viewed as supportive for prices. "It was a confirmation that it is still a tight situation," he said.

The Green Coffee Association of New York reported late Tuesday that supplies of green coffee stored in U.S. warehouses rose in January by a modest 15,000 bags, to 1.264 million bags. Traders were also keeping an eye on Colombia, where a
powerful earthquake rocked the central-western region of the country Wednesday.

While there was no immediate news of serious damage or injuries, Colombian national radio reported minor damage, including broken windows in Pereira and Armenia, cities in the heart of the country's central coffee-growing region.
NYMEX gasoline rose Wednesday in early anticipation of its seasonal spring rally before the summer driving season.
"You have some guys getting into gasoline early because while people are looking for this market to bottom, they also don't want to miss the rally," said Prudential Securities trader Mike DeLuca.
March gasoline ended up 0.52 cent a gallon at 64.68 cents.
March heating oil ended up 0.17 cent a gallon at 59.59 cents while March crude finished up 27 cents a barrel at $22.79.
Dealers said crude prices may give up their gains Thursday do to weekly oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API), which was reported Wednesday after the market's close.
"The API's (data) should certainly be on the bearish side (for crude)," said a dealer, noting a healthy buildup in crude stocks. The data reflects the week ended last Friday.
The API reported crude stocks grew a healthy 3.12 million barrels, in line with expectations, while gasoline stocks showed a surprising decline.

The API said gasoline stocks dropped 1.27 million barrels when traders had been expecting a buildup of about 1 million barrels. Distillate stocks, which reflect heating oil and diesel, fell 2.90 million barrels, in line with expectations.
